description: Somos un equipo de estudiantes de Ingeniería de Sistemas comprometidos con la innovación y el desarrollo de soluciones tecnológicas para desafíos reales. En el NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, buscamos crear un software de monitorización de la salud de astronautas que facilite el seguimiento de sus indicadores de salud, la detección temprana de cambios y la toma de decisiones durante misiones espaciales de larga duración.
summary:
ASTRO-VITALS is an autonomous health monitoring system designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It collects and analyzes physiological and environmental telemetry to identify unusual patterns, assess potential risks, and provide timely, explainable guidance without requiring continuous communication with Earth.

The system combines personalized baselines, sensor-quality assessment, rule-based analysis, and predictive models to monitor relevant indicators such as heart rate, radiation exposure, and cabin CO₂ levels. Its local-first architecture allows continuous operation and real-time monitoring, even when communication with Earth is unavailable.

ASTRO-VITALS aims to help astronauts understand changes in their health and environment, recognize potential warning signs, and make better-informed decisions during demanding missions. It is designed as a decision-support tool, not as a replacement for professional medical diagnosis.
details:
ASTRO-VITALS: Local-First Astronaut Health and Environmental Monitoring Prototype

What the project does and how it works

ASTRO-VITALS is a software prototype for exploring how crew health signals and spacecraft environmental context could be reviewed together during a space mission. It processes telemetry locally and presents it in a web-based monitoring console and a terminal interface. The current prototype runs on a computer; it is not flight-qualified and is not connected to spacecraft or medical sensors.

The system establishes a resting reference using the median and median absolute deviation (MAD), then evaluates incoming signals for sustained changes. A machine-learning model estimates heart rate about 60 seconds ahead; when its inputs are insufficient, the system uses a simple persistence-based reference. A separate classifier looks for four physiological patterns using 30- and 120-second windows. That classifier was trained with synthetic scenarios, not astronaut records. When data are missing, stale, or insufficient, the prototype preserves missing values and can abstain instead of presenting an unsupported assessment.

For cabin context, the CO₂ module analyzes recent trends with ordinary least squares (OLS) and estimates sensitivity and time to a configured reference threshold when enough data are available. Thresholds depend on the selected demonstration environment; they should not be interpreted as operational NASA limits.

The radiation module integrates valid dose-rate readings over time. DONKI supplies historical solar-event context, while the local dosimeter readings and shelter-effectiveness factor are simulated separately. The prototype does not calculate real spacecraft shielding or personal exposure from the historical event.

The console also includes a seven-zone monitoring view, scenario controls, behavioral check-ins, crew routines, privacy settings, and downloadable SBAR-style reports. These are interaction and situational-awareness features, not clinical services.

Benefits and intended impact

ASTRO-VITALS demonstrates a local-first approach: the prototype can process and display data without depending on a continuous connection to Earth. It brings physiological trends, cabin conditions, data quality, and event context into one place, so a crew member can review what changed and what information is missing.

The intended impact is to explore design ideas for more autonomous crew awareness during long-duration missions, including communication outages. This prototype has not been clinically or operationally validated, and it does not diagnose, replace medical professionals, or establish that it improves astronaut health outcomes.

Data sources and validation

  • NASA DONKI: historical solar-event information used for context, not as a personal radiation measurement.
  • BIDMC PPG and Respiration Dataset: physiological data used for heart-rate forecasting development and available for replay in the prototype.
  • Synthetic cohort: controlled examples used to train and exercise the physiological-pattern classifier.
  • NASA RR-1 and other terrestrial datasets, including PPG-DaLiA, WESAD, and MMASH: additional historical or terrestrial reference data in the project. They are not astronaut measurements and do not establish in-space model performance.

The project includes automated tests for data contracts, analytical behavior, model components, and end-to-end flows. Testing verifies software behavior, not medical efficacy or readiness for spaceflight.

Tools and technology

The backend and analysis engine use Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, and Uvicorn. SQLite provides local persistence; WebSockets and REST APIs carry updates to the interface. NumPy and scikit-learn support statistical and machine-learning components, with Joblib for model artifacts. The web console uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Canvas; the terminal interface uses Textual. Pytest is used for automated testing. No custom hardware or in-flight sensor integration is part of the current prototype.

What is creative and what the team considered

The project combines personalized baselines, short-term forecasting, environmental trends, historical space-weather context, and simulated dosimetry in a single locally operating demonstration. It distinguishes historical context from simulated measurements, accounts for missing or stale data, and can abstain rather than treating gaps as zero. Privacy, local operation during communication interruptions, clear evidence, and the limitations of terrestrial and synthetic datasets shaped the design.

ASTRO-VITALS is an experimental prototype intended to support discussion and further research into crew-centered monitoring for future exploration—not a validated medical or spacecraft system.
